results.explanationEn: Early in the letter, Benedita writes that her brother has not opened his grammar book once since Bruno left. She then makes clear that she has not forgiven Bruno's words, but adds that her brother has become so listless that he hasn't memorized a single verb in six weeks and doesn't even back away from the smoke of the bees. Putting the two clues together, she calls Bruno back because of her brother's listlessness, so the answer is B. A describes a feeling that is the opposite of the text, and C and D bring in outside causes that the text never mentions.

Thorvald's brother has already died, and when the narrator says someone in the family could read the letter, Thorvald shakes his head. Combined with the earlier description of him looking toward the water as if waiting for a boat that would not come, this shows that an apology is complete only when someone on the other side is there to receive it, so the answer is D. A reverses the order of forgiveness, and B relies only on the act of burning the letter and mistakes it for secrecy. C does not fit the fact that he had already written the letter.

The text first gives the background that city planners faced the problem of congested streets, then in the underlined sentence explains that some planners proposed a solution: elevated railways. The following sentences develop the story by describing the benefits of this solution (cheap, fast construction) and the problems that came later (noise, shadows, damaged aesthetics). The underlined sentence therefore serves to present a proposed solution to a problem, and the answer is A. B is wrong because it is the end of the text, not the underlined sentence, that summarizes the debate's outcome, so it confuses the timing. C is wrong because the sentence after the underlined one actually supports the underlined claim (elevated railways really were cheap and fast), so it reverses the cause-and-effect relationship. D is wrong because the proposal came from the planners themselves, not from opponents making a concession, so it confuses who is speaking.

Correct answer B (watched): The quotation describes a repeated routine from her past apprenticeship, and the verbs that share the subject I are listed in parallel as swept, sorted, ___. So the third verb must also be in the simple past, watched, to match in both tense and form.
A (have watched): The present perfect does not fit the past point in time of the quotation (the year she spent, Each morning ... swept), which refers to a finished year in the past. It conflicts with the tense of the quotation.
C (was watching): The past time frame is right, but it is the only progressive form among the parallel items, so it does not match swept and sorted. It is wrong because it changes the form of just one item in a parallel structure.
D (watch): This seems to match the present tense of the sentence surrounding the quotation (notes, shapes, trains today). However, the blank sits where the past routine inside the quotation is being listed, so it does not fit the overall context.

Benedita leaves the previous teacher's chalk marks as they are and never mentions the empty chair, and she learns from Dariush how to hold the tape measure the way that teacher did and imitates it exactly. Dariush, who at first answered in only one word, later starts arriving early to sweep up loose threads. Putting the two clues together, the answer is C. A reflects only his early wariness, B exaggerates by reversing the direction of the teaching, and D is a relationship chosen from the stereotype of a strict teacher.

The narrator fondly recalls the feeling of walking back across the salt flat, the triumphant mood, and the old man folding the newspaper as if giving a gift. She says the small sting of the lie is still there, but that she remembers 'mostly' the old man's kind touch. So the answer is A, fond nostalgia mixed with a faint sense of guilt. B reverses the proportions, C names only the less prominent emotion, and D fits the subject of a stranger but has weak support in the text.

The text says the two do not talk about Suhyun's solo contract and talk about the bridge instead. It then repeats scenes of one of them touching the crack that was filled long ago as if checking it every night, and of Suhyun resting her hand on it for a long time the day before the deadline. Putting these clues together, the crack and the mortar symbolize the duo's relationship, barely held together by what goes unsaid, so the answer is D. A uses the surface detail of shrinking audiences, B takes the crack literally, and C has no basis in the text.

The sentence before the blank describes research findings that microbial diversity has a positive effect on drought resilience and crop yield, and the sentence after the blank describes the action that followed as a result: agricultural support programs actually began adopting microbial diversity assessments. The first sentence is the cause and the second is its result, so 'Consequently,', which signals cause and effect, is the most logical choice. 'However,' signals contrast, 'For example,' signals an example, and 'Nevertheless,' signals concession, but the two sentences are in a cause-and-effect relationship, not a contrast or concession, so they are not appropriate. The answer is C.

Early on, Odile points out that Genevieve softened 'hid' into 'was careful,' and she demands that the letter be read 'not in polite words but exactly as her mother wrote it.' Later, when Odile says her mother has sounded small all this time, Genevieve answers that she will do it properly this time. Putting the two parts together, this is a scene of a client pressing her interpreter to convey her mother's voice faithfully, so the answer is B. A summarizes only the event that set things off, C is wrong because no legal process is explained, and D is an overly general moral.

Janelle deliberately withdrew her entry so that Shanice, the narrator, would win, she does not take the ribbon back, and she says the garden must learn Shanice's name. Shanice keeps the ribbon in a drawer instead of hanging it on the wall, and each time she sees it she tends the garden more carefully, as if the prize were still being judged. Putting the two clues together, the ribbon is a sign of welcome that Shanice has accepted but still feels she must prove herself worthy of, so the answer is C. B and D misread the win as skill or pride, and A does not fit Janelle's generous act.

First, the slope of R is (460-340)/(4-0) = 30, so R(t) = 30t + 340. R(10) = 30(10)+340 = 640, so ridership can reach 700 only after t=10. From t=10 on, the growth rate is half, 15, and the value 640 at t=10 carries over, so solving 640 + 15(t-10) = 700 gives 15(t-10) = 60, t-10 = 4, t = 14. So the answer is C.

The student's goal is to explain why the Venus flytrap needs two touches. The correct answer accurately connects the two-touch mechanism (Note 3) with the reason it exists, not wasting energy on non-food objects (Note 4), completing the cause-and-effect relationship. Each wrong answer misses the goal in a different way: the second choice mentions only the trigger mechanism itself (Note 2) and does not address the reason for 'why two'; the third wrongly combines the digestion period (Note 5), an unrelated detail, as if it were the reason for two touches; and the fourth wrongly presents the habitat (Note 1), an unrelated detail, as the cause.

Early on, the mother laughs and teases her son by listing the birdhouse and the many projects he never finished. After she finds, under the birdhouse, the roof measurements he wrote down when he was little, she stops talking and sets the birdhouse down carefully. So the tone shifts from playful teasing to quiet tenderness, and the answer is B. A does not fit the laughter at the start, C is wrong because she teased her son instead of boasting about his skill, and D is wrong because no irritation about the packing appears.

The previous sentence explains that insects slip down the slippery inner wall into a pool of digestive fluid, and after the blank the text adds that this happens 'with minimal energy.' This means the plant traps and holds its prey through its physical structure alone, so capture is the most appropriate choice. Digest is the next step of processing prey that has already been caught, not the capturing process; attract means luring insects in, which differs from the situation of slipping and being trapped; and release means the opposite of the context.

The early use of the title 'Maestro' and the courtesy of standing up show only the formal conductor-and-player relationship (A). In the middle, Ruoxi hasn't opened the gas bill for nearly a year, yet the stove keeps running, and later come the small expense records marked with a T and the shelf where the bills have disappeared. These reveal that Tyrese has been quietly paying for the house's costs. So the one who has quietly paid is Tyrese, and the answer is D. B reflects only the documented fact of 'overdue rent,' and C reads the ledger merely as neat records, reversing the direction of dependence.

Painter M: the slope is $(80-30)/(10-0)=5$ and the intercept is 30, so $y=5x+30$. Painter K: the slope is $(70-90)/(20-0)=-1$ and the intercept is 90, so $y=-x+90$. Setting them equal: $5x+30=-x+90$, $6x=60$, $x=10$. Since $x$ is the number of years since 1990, the year is $1990+10=2000$. The graph also confirms that the two lines intersect at $x=10$. The answer is 2000.

Correct answer C: The text's broad claim is that even if the sagas' plots are fictional, read together with excavated evidence they can contain reliable knowledge about everyday economic practices, and the change in the bone ratios at the farmstead is a case supporting this claim. C summarizes exactly this scope.
A (too narrow): It states only one detail, the change in bone ratios, and omits the main point that this is evidence for the sagas' reliability.
B (too broad): The text deals only with the Icelandic sagas, and only with their content about everyday economics. The claim that northern European literature in general is accurate goes beyond the text's scope.
D (mixed scope): It blends the broad claim with a detail and distorts the facts. The text clearly says that the feud narratives are not supported by the site, so saying the feuds were also confirmed is wrong.

Faris wraps the gift with great care and looks only at the narrator's hands, not the scarf, then lets out a sigh of relief and pours out his words in a rush; these are clues that he is very concerned about the narrator's reaction. The narrator, even though it is a color she dislikes, ties on the scarf and compliments it, and asks a question after each of his reports to ease his tension. A invents irritation on the narrator's part, and B reverses the direction of the relationship. In C, the joke belongs to the brother and does not show an old friendship between the two, so D is the answer.

In its first sentence the text states that the light organ is 'only one part of a broader survival strategy,' and then lists the jaws, the stomach, and the light organ together, explaining that they all work together to help the fish survive in a food-scarce environment. The correct answer captures this overall main idea: that several traits work together. The first wrong answer (only how the light organ works) is a detail mentioned in the text but is too narrow because it focuses on a single adaptive trait (TOO_NARROW_DETAIL). The second wrong answer (features of the deep-sea environment itself) is only background and does not address the anglerfish's adaptations, so the focus is off (WRONG_FOCUS). The third wrong answer overgeneralizes a detail about a single adaptive trait, the stomach, as if it were the key conclusion of the whole text, excluding the other two traits (the jaws and the light organ), so it is an overgeneralization error (OVERGENERALIZED).

In the first part, the narrator thinks Albert foolish for repeatedly breaking kite frames when a child would not even know the difference. But after seeing him on the night before the feast day trimming ribs he had already trimmed twice, the narrator recalls that from then on she tried to keep even small promises. Through the contrast between these two passages, D shows how the narrator came to value the master's care for a promise that seemed trivial, so D is the answer. A summarizes the anecdote, B shares the subject matter but not the purpose, and C is an overly general moral.

The key point of the text is that the octopus's short lifespan is due not to simple biological frailty but to a specific hormonal program triggered by the optic gland. A summarizes this causal relationship accurately. B is only background information in the opening of the text and not the main idea (WRONG_FOCUS); C overstates the scope with 'always' and generalizes the detail that the female dies before the eggs hatch (OVERGENERALIZED); and D is merely a detail about the experimental method, expanded into a 'commonly used technique,' which is too narrow a view (TOO_NARROW_DETAIL).

In this sentence the main verb of the main clause is 'evolved,' and its subject is 'the plants' waxy inner walls.' The modifying phrase inserted between commas must not create another complete verb competing with the main verb, so it should be handled as added description using the participle 'remaining.'

'remain' is a finite verb form, so it conflicts with the existing main verb 'evolved,' creating an error in which two verbs sit side by side without a conjunction (a structure like a comma splice).

'they remain' adds an unnecessary subject and makes an independent clause, creating an error in which a clause is attached without a conjunction in a slot meant for a comma-set-off inserted phrase.

'having remained being' is an unnecessarily wordy and ungrammatical verb phrase; the participial phrase itself breaks down in form and creates an awkward dangling modifier that does not attach smoothly to 'the plants' waxy inner walls.'

So the answer is C.

Correct answer B: Arakawa's hypothesis is a causal chain: food supply right after hatching leads to development of the song-control brain regions, which leads to song complexity. B uses brothers (with similar genetic backgrounds) and shows that when food was experimentally restricted right after hatching, the brain regions became smaller and the songs simpler, directly confirming each link in this chain, so it most directly supports the hypothesis.
A (a fact unrelated to the hypothesis): The result that feeding in adulthood did not affect song contradicts nothing, but it shows nothing about the key claim that early feeding determines song. For example, the same result would appear even if song complexity were determined by genetics alone, regardless of food. The overlapping phrase 'developmental window' makes it look plausible.
C (restatement of the text): That adult males differ greatly in song complexity is an observation already given in the last sentence of the text, and it does not show whether that difference came from nutrition in early life.
D (a result that refutes the hypothesis): If song complexity was the same even when early food was restricted, that weakens the claim that early nutrition determines song complexity.

Early on, Paloma creates a playful mood by handing over the key as if presenting a crown and trading jokes about the new job. But from the moment she holds the water-test vial longer than necessary, she slowly explains the pool's history and the winter drain trick, and her tone becomes serious and quiet. So the answer is D. A conflicts with the description that Paloma neither holds the narrator back nor blames her, B shows no resolve on the narrator's part, and C reads the order of the change backward.

After her husband's death, Eda has shoes that no one will wear repaired three times and sets them by the door. Comparing this to 'stitching a new sentence onto a closed book' means an attempt to add something to a life that has already ended, so the answer is B. A does not fit the description that the cobbler did the work without complaint, and C reads 'book' literally as a record. D conflicts with the fact that she repeatedly asks for the repairs herself.

Correct answer B experimentally manipulates temperature and shows the development period shrinking dramatically, so it most directly supports the causal claim that low temperature lowers metabolic rate and slows development. A is a behavioral observation that the mother never leaves her eggs, which could even emphasize a behavioral factor and points in a different direction from the authors' claim of 'temperature, not behavior.' C is evidence that refutes the claim that temperature is the cause, since a similarly long brooding period appeared in a warm place. D is a difference in egg size, a detail unrelated to development time, so it does not support the claim.

The subject of this sentence is the singular noun 'this shift,' and since past-tense verbs such as 'spent' and 'incorporated' have already been used in the earlier clause, the verb must also be in the past tense and singular. 'made' is the only choice that meets all of these conditions. 'making' is a participle, not a verb, so it cannot fill the main-verb slot and leaves the sentence incomplete. 'have made' suits a plural subject or a present-perfect context and does not agree in number with the singular subject 'this shift.' 'makes, and' is in the present tense, causing a tense mismatch, and the unnecessary conjunction muddles the sentence boundary.

The fellow nurses teased that the cranes were a sign that he wanted something, but the request the narrator waited for never came. Even on the last night, Grant only asked whether she had kept the cranes and smiled, and the narrator left the cranes on the windowsill for a long time. Putting this together, the cranes are a sign of gratitude offered without expecting anything in return, so the answer is A. B simply follows the colleagues' suspicion, and C's boredom and D's teasing interpret the cranes' meaning only at the level of subject matter.

The narrator sarcastically calls Philip's names for him, such as 'reptile,' 'equally agreeable names.' He also says the girl 'done me the honour' of choosing him, showing an attitude entirely unmoved by Philip's anger. So the answer is A. B's shame, C's fear, and D's sympathy have no basis in the text.

Ephraim declines the invitation politely but at length, yet in the underlined sentence he sweeps the fountain clean even though it has no water. This hints at a care he does not put into words, and later the knot placed in the middle of the fountain, instead of the plate the narrator left, becomes his indirect reply. So the answer is C. A's plan to restore the fountain, B's quarrel, and D's disconnection among residents have no basis in the text.

The previous sentence says that researchers made long breeding and relocation efforts to save the baiji, and the sentence after the blank reports the result that, despite those efforts, the 2006 survey did not find a single animal. This is a result that runs against the earlier efforts, so 'Nevertheless,', which signals concession, is the most logical. B introduces an example, but the sentence that follows is not an instance of the previous content but a contrary result, so it is wrong. C signals similarity, but the two sentences describe contrasting, not similar, situations, so it is wrong. D seems to signal contrast, but it is usually used when comparing two parallel subjects, and here the nuance of concession, 'despite the earlier efforts,' is more accurate.

The narrator says Valentina dislikes her and points out how she folds laundry and seasons food. But Valentina goes to the post office first every morning and brings back news, and the narrator, seeing her fall asleep while mending the narrator's blouse, recognizes the care beneath her blunt manner. Respect also shows in the narrator folding clothes the way Valentina prefers, so the answer is D. A reflects only the early impression, and B and C have no basis in the text.

In the early part, Kaya calls Nneka 'an impossible person' and complains in two languages that the heel repairs are unnecessary. The hesitant correction 'not pleasant, not quite' in the middle hints that the complaint is not the whole story. Even after hearing that she is being replaced, Kaya goes to the shop alone, prepays a month of heel repairs, and leaves the receipt in Nneka's name, an act that keeps their shared Friday habit going. So the answer is D. A reads only the tone of speech, B swaps guilt in as the reason for the affection, and C generalizes toward complaint alone by borrowing the text's heel-repair wording.

Lucy flatly states that she has had no love story and that it is now too late, and she feels tired and lonely. She merely thinks it would be 'quite nice' to be adored by Perry, so the tone is resigned, and the answer is A. B's joy does not fit the absence of love, and C's anger and D's mockery conflict with the fact that she actually pities Perry.

Reading together the scene of Kamal secretly paying Xiulan's fare and only studying the timetable, and the scene of Xiulan silently setting soy milk beside him and Kamal merely nodding, we see a long-standing affection in which they exchange care without words. The old habit of putting water beside the music stand also shows that the relationship goes back a long way. So the answer is D. A sees only Kamal's avoidance of eye contact and misreads one side; B uses the text's vocabulary but reverses the direction of who paid the fare; and C is a stereotype about people who once shared a stage.

Early on, Emiliano acts like an experienced resident, telling her about the garden plots, the leaky faucet, and the neighbors' temperaments. Later he signs in the new-member column right below Ximena and holds the pen for a long time, revealing that he too was just starting out. Connecting the two events, the main idea is the irony in D: the confident guidance came from someone almost as unfamiliar as she was. A summarizes only Event 1 and B only Event 2, and C creates a causal link, advice causing the sign-up, thereby misreading the relationship between the two events.

The student's claim has two parts: (1) the lower the temperature, the longer the shelf life (a consistent direction), and (2) the size of the increase differs from interval to interval. B accurately cites from the table the difference between 2°C and 6°C (7 days) and the difference between 10°C and 14°C (8 days), showing that the direction is consistent (shelf life increases as temperature falls) but the size differs, so it supports both parts of the claim. A picks a case where the two intervals happen to have the same difference (both 7 days) and wrongly concludes that the size of the increase is constant, supporting the opposite of the claim. C compares only two points (18°C and 6°C), so it shows the direction but is not a comparison between adjacent temperature intervals, and it proves neither the continuous relationship of 'the lower the temperature' nor the second part, that the size varies. D shows that the size of the decrease differs, but it covers only the decrease as temperature rises, not the direction of the student's claim (the temperature-shelf life relationship), so its framing conflicts with the claim's wording (increases when lowered).

The answer is C. The narrator asks Nova only whether she can tell bean seeds from pumpkin seeds and does not press her for a reason, and says she trusts the truth that comes later more than a long confession. At the same time, the narrator watches carefully as Nova sets the envelope with her grandmother's handwriting aside and as she writes labels in similar handwriting. A mistakes observation for suspicion, B misses that it is Yona, not the narrator, who raised her eyebrows, and D has no basis for the hope that she will return to Mass.

The narrator at first 'said' she resented Mateo, but upon learning that he secretly oils the pendulum every dawn, she cannot sustain her anger. She then comes to understand that her brother's restlessness is another form of loyalty, born of not wanting to watch the shop fail. Putting the two clues together, this is an attitude of growing sympathy for hidden motives, so the answer is B. A reflects only her early feeling, C is wrong because no amusement appears in the text, and D has no basis for the claim that Mateo will stay.

The student's goal is to explain how the light indirectly protects the dinoflagellates from predation. To do this, one must combine (1) the relationship in which copepods are predators of the dinoflagellates, and (2) the 'indirect' causal relationship, separate from the light startling the copepods directly, in which the light draws in larger predators that then eat the copepods (the burglar alarm hypothesis). D combines these two relationships accurately and explains 'indirect protection.' A mentions visitors, unrelated to the chemical reaction process, so it is irrelevant to the goal (IGNORES_GOAL). B covers only the other notes, nutrient runoff and boat restrictions, and is unrelated to protection from predation (it resembles MISUSES_ONE_NOTE_ONLY but is also off the goal, a digression). C combines the first defense mechanism, 'directly' startling the copepods, with the chemical reaction note, but this explains 'direct' protection, not 'indirect' protection, so it conflicts with the goal (COMBINES_WRONG_NOTES). So the answer is D.
